questions.q: In data parallelism, what does each GPU replica hold and process?
options: A different slice of the model's layers, processing the same batch
A full copy of the entire model, processing a different micro-batch of data
Only the optimizer state, with weights stored on a separate server
A compressed version of the model to save memory
questions.explain: Data parallelism replicates the full model onto every GPU. Each replica processes its own different micro-batch of data independently.

questions.q: What operation keeps every data-parallel replica's weights identical after each training step?
options: A random weight swap between GPUs
An all-reduce that averages gradients across all replicas before any weight update is applied
Each replica independently decides its own learning rate
Replicas are re-initialized from scratch every step
questions.explain: An all-reduce sums (or averages) each parameter's gradient across every replica and writes the result back to all of them, so every replica applies the identical update.

questions.q: What memory problem does plain data parallelism fail to solve?
options: It increases memory usage on every GPU compared to single-GPU training
Every replica still holds a full copy of the weights, gradients, and optimizer state, so a model that doesn't fit on one GPU still won't fit
It eliminates the need for an optimizer entirely
It requires storing the dataset in GPU memory permanently
questions.explain: Data parallelism does not shard the model, gradients, or optimizer state across GPUs -- it only replicates them. A model too large for one GPU remains too large under plain DP.

questions.q: In PyTorch's DistributedDataParallel (DDP) setup, what is the role of DistributedSampler?
options: It compresses the dataset to reduce disk usage
It ensures each process's DataLoader sees a disjoint shard of the dataset rather than duplicated data
It automatically tunes the learning rate for multi-GPU training
It synchronizes gradients across GPUs instead of all-reduce
questions.explain: DistributedSampler partitions the dataset so each process in the distributed job processes a different shard, avoiding redundant computation on duplicated data.

questions.q: How does global batch size relate to the number of data-parallel replicas?
options: Global batch size is unrelated to the number of replicas
Global batch size equals the per-GPU micro-batch size divided by the number of replicas
Global batch size equals the per-GPU micro-batch size multiplied by the number of replicas (times any gradient accumulation steps)
Global batch size is always fixed at 1 regardless of replica count
questions.explain: Because each replica consumes its own micro-batch per step, the effective global batch size scales with the number of replicas, times any gradient accumulation steps used on top.
